title: Empathetic exclamatory situation framing
description: This latent fires on stock empathetic openers that exclaim over the difficulty of the user's situation, typically of the form 'What a [adjective] and [adjective] situation/feeling/dilemma!' or 'That can be a [adjective] and [adjective] situation.' It responds specifically to this templated validating exclamation pattern -- pairing two emotionally-loaded adjectives (complex, sensitive, challenging, painful, emotional, heartbreaking) with a noun like situation, feeling, dilemma, or concern -- used as an empathy-signaling preamble before advice-giving. It does not activate on general empathetic or supportive statements that lack this exclamatory adjective-pair template (e.g., 'I'm so sorry to hear that,' 'It's completely understandable that...', or substantive advice/analysis sentences), even though those may express similar sentiment through different phrasing.

title: Defining a category of abuse
description: This latent activates on sentences that introduce and define a specific type or category of abusive/harmful behavior, typically in a term-plus-definition format (e.g., 'X: Using/doing Y'). It responds to concise, categorical labeling of a harmful behavior followed by a clarifying description of what that behavior entails, often as part of a list or taxonomy of abuse types. It would not activate on narrative descriptions of abuse occurring in a specific instance, personal accounts of being abused, or general discussion of abuse's effects/consequences without the defining, label-plus-explanation structure.

title: Reassuring self-worth affirmations
description: This latent fires on formulaic, therapeutic-style affirmations that directly address 'you' with validating statements about deserving happiness, respect, love, or well-being, and imperative encouragements to prioritize self-care, healing, or boundary-setting. It activates most strongly on short, template-like phrases such as 'You deserve to be...', 'Remember, you deserve...', 'Take care of yourself and prioritize your own...', and 'Keep...' that read like closing lines of advice-column or chatbot responses offering comfort and permission for self-focus. It is weaker or inactive on sentences that give situational analysis, ask questions, list numbered options, or discuss the other person's behavior/motives, even if they occur in the same supportive advice-giving context, since the latent specifically tracks the direct affirming/validating address to the reader rather than general relationship advice or reasoning.

title: Token 'Don' detection
description: This latent activates on the specific token fragment "Don", most likely appearing at the very start of a sentence or clause. It seems to respond to this token whether it functions as the beginning of a proper name (e.g., "Don" as in Don Smith) or as the start of a contraction like "Don't", capturing the raw lexical form rather than its semantic role. Given only a single truncated example, the latent appears keyed to surface-level token identity rather than a broader reasoning pattern or topic. It would not activate on sentences that discuss similar names or negations without using this exact token string, nor on the word "Don" embedded mid-sentence in contexts clearly distinguishable by surrounding punctuation or capitalization patterns not seen here.

title: List-item enumeration markers
description: This latent fires on the numeric or short lead-in tokens that begin an enumerated list item, such as isolated '2.', '3.', '4.' markers, or short list-preamble fragments like 'Consider', 'By', or 'By communicating' that introduce a bulleted/numbered suggestion. It activates most strongly on the bare numbering token itself (the list marker in isolation), and more weakly within full sentences that begin a list item or introduce a step in an advice sequence. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences that lack list structure, or on numbers used in non-enumeration contexts (e.g., dates, quantities, statistics) since the trigger is specifically the structural role of beginning a new list item or step, not the numeral's semantic content.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (e.g. "2.", "3.", "4.") that serve as bullet/list item markers in enumerated advice or reasoning lists, typically in AITA-style responses breaking down points into numbered steps. It activates most strongly on the bare digit-plus-period token itself, largely independent of surrounding content, and secondarily on nearby sentences within such structured, judgmental (e.g. 'unreasonable', 'entitled') list-based responses. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking list numbering, or on list markers rendered as bolded headers without a plain numeral, since the core trigger is the literal enumeration marker rather than the semantic content being enumerated.

title: Suggested opening lines for checking in / initiating a personal conversation
description: This latent fires on template phrases—often modeled as quoted or suggested dialogue ('You could say something like...', 'You might say...')—that open an emotionally-laden interpersonal conversation, especially check-ins on someone's wellbeing ('Is everything okay?', 'Have you been feeling okay?') or invitations to talk/hang out ('Can we talk about something on my mind?', 'Would you guys be free to grab dinner?'). It activates most strongly on short, first/second-person conversational openers and softening phrases used to broach a sensitive topic or propose meeting up, including repeated stock phrases like 'Is everything okay?' and 'I wanted to talk to you about something that's been on my mind.' It does NOT activate on advice/analysis content that discusses relationship dynamics in the third person or gives general strategic recommendations (e.g., 'Respect her boundaries', 'Try inhaling for a count of 4', 'It's possible she felt embarrassed'), since those are explanatory/advisory statements rather than modeled conversation-starting utterances.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the digit token that marks a position in an enumerated list (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.**'), regardless of the list's topic or content. It activates most strongly on isolated numeral tokens beginning a list item, often followed by a period and/or bold-markdown asterisks, and appears across advice lists, step-by-step instructions, and bulleted reasoning. It does not activate on the textual content of list items themselves, on prose sentences without enumeration, or on numbers used as quantities or dates rather than as list markers.

title: Suggesting practical alternative solutions
description: This latent fires on bullet-style or list-item suggestions that propose concrete alternative options, compromises, or arrangements for resolving a practical problem—typically financial, logistical, or scheduling issues like rent, bills, childcare, transportation, or payment plans. The activating sentences follow a pattern of 'consider/explore/offer X or Y' where multiple discrete options are enumerated as advice, often in an advice-column or problem-solving context. It is strongest on terse, formulaic advice bullets (e.g., 'Explore alternative arrangements, such as...' or 'Consider a temporary arrangement where...') that explicitly name a fallback or compromise option. It does NOT activate strongly on general empathetic commentary, open-ended questions, moral judgments about a situation, or narrative/descriptive sentences that don't propose a specific alternative course of action, even if they appear in the same advice-giving context.

title: Benefit-of-social-action framing
description: This latent activates on sentences that state the interpersonal benefit or payoff of performing a suggested social action, typically phrased as 'This can/will help you [achieve some relational or emotional outcome]', such as building rapport, feeling comfortable, or connecting with others. It responds to concise, advice-style statements that justify a prior recommendation by naming its positive social or emotional effect. It would not activate on sentences that merely give an instruction without stating its benefit, on purely factual or descriptive statements, or on benefit statements about non-social/practical outcomes (e.g., saving money, improving efficiency) that lack an interpersonal or emotional dimension.

title: Prompting self-reflective trigger identification
description: This latent fires on directive sentences that instruct the reader to identify or reflect on personal triggers, causes, or antecedents of an emotion or behavior (e.g., 'identify the situations, people, or emotions that trigger X'). It activates on imperative, self-help or therapeutic-style prompts that ask someone to introspect and enumerate contributing factors to a psychological or behavioral state. It would not activate on general descriptive statements about emotions, factual explanations of causes, or advice-giving sentences that don't use an instructional/imperative framing directed at self-analysis.

title: AITA verdict-seeking question
description: This latent fires on the literal closing catchphrase of r/AmItheAsshole-style posts, specifically the formulaic 'So, AITA?' (or 'Am I the asshole?') question that a narrator poses at the end of recounting a personal conflict story to solicit a moral judgment from readers. It activates most strongly on this exact tag-question phrasing, and more weakly on related verdict-related phrasing like 'So, NTA' or 'are you the Asshole?' that invoke the same judgment-request convention. It does not activate on the surrounding advice-giving content, sympathetic responses, or actual verdicts/explanations (e.g., 'you're not the asshole because...'), which instead reflect other latents concerned with reassurance, reasoning, or suggestion-giving rather than the ritualized question itself.

title: Endorsing positive coping strategies
description: This latent activates on statements that recommend or affirm a simple behavior or mindset shift (like laughter, exercise, or gratitude) as a means of improving mood, perspective, or well-being. It fires on general, upbeat advisory claims framing an activity as beneficial for emotional or mental state, often using words like 'can be a great way to.' It would not activate on neutral factual statements, narrow technical descriptions, or negative/cautionary statements that don't frame something as a positive coping mechanism.
